newsitem.title: PERU: Exultant Fujimori offers help for crises abroad.
newsitem.headline: Exultant Fujimori offers help for crises abroad.

text.p: Peru did not receive any foreign help in crushing Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence, and is ready to offer advice to foreign governments that face similar crises, President Alberto Fujimori said on Friday.

"There was no American, British, Israeli or Japanese advice. None at all. Rather, in the future we can give advice to countries who keep facing these problems," he told Reuters in his first interview after Tuesday's spectacular military rescue operation.
Eagerly recounting the non-secret details of the raid, Fujimori said his greatest pride in this "imaginative solution" was that it was an entirely local operation.
"This was a knockout blow from 'creole' technology, as we say in Peru," Fujimori said.

Although refusing to reveal how security forces smuggled into the home bugging devices and other electronic gadgets used to alert hostages of the attack, Fujimori revealed that a key element was "four, ultra-light periscopes" poked out of tunnels built under the compound.
"One of the tunnels has a large mouth seven yards (meters) deep. There was a complete system of stairs with cords," he said.

The tunnels were inspired by the "brilliant" architecture of the 3,000-year-old Chavin de Huantar complex in northern Peru, Fujimori said. The idea to name the operation after this complex came to him in the middle of the night.
He said that the decision to enter the residence was taken on Sunday because of the increasing "risk of an incident, a bloody incident."
"The situation inside the residence could not be tolerated any longer," he added.
